title: Sunset without objects
hook: arti with nothing but the actual sun

segments.voice: Yesterday, family arti: a job for everyone in the house. Your line was one more. Did you ask one more person to join something? Day one hundred and twenty-three.

You're in a hospital waiting room. Or an airport. Or a dorm where candles are banned, or a friend's house, or a work trip in a hotel with a window that doesn't open. No shelf, no lamp, no bell, no flower. It's evening, and this week's arti has nowhere to happen. So here's today's question. If you took away every object from this week, the lamp, the plate, the camphor, the song sheet, what would be left? One answer is right there. Look out the window. Today: sunset without objects.
screen: `NO SHELF, NO LAMP, NO BELL.` → `WHAT'S LEFT?` → `LOOK OUT THE WINDOW.`

segments.voice: Long before there were brass lamps and printed arti songs, there were the Vedas. And the very first hymn of the Rig Veda is to Agni, fire, praised as the priest of the sacrifice, the one who carries offerings to the gods. Other hymns sing to the dawn, and to the sun. The Gayatri, from day one hundred and eight, asks the light of the sun to wake up the mind. The sun has a special title in Hindu tradition: it's sometimes called the god you can actually see. You don't need an image to imagine it; it's right there, every day, rising and setting. Here's one way to see the arti lamp. Every evening, as the sun goes down, a household lights a small flame and holds it up. The little flame is a kind of stand-in for the big one, carried indoors for the night. The sun is the original flame. And that means, when you have nothing, you still have it. On day one hundred and fifteen, water was poured toward the sun at dawn. At dusk, you can simply turn west, where the sun is setting, put your hands together, and watch. That's the whole ritual: the light that crossed the sky all day, finishing its path in front of you. One practical thing. Never stare straight into the sun. Watch the sky around it, the colors, the edges of the clouds. The light will find your face without your help.
screen: `THE RIG VEDA OPENS WITH FIRE.` · `THE GOD YOU CAN ACTUALLY SEE.` · `THE LAMP IS A STAND-IN.` · `FACE WEST. HANDS TOGETHER. WATCH.`

segments.voice: If you can, turn toward the west, toward a window, or where the sun sets even if it's hidden right now. If it's not evening, picture the last sunset you remember well. Put your hands together at your chest, if you'd like. Don't look at the sun itself; look at the sky around it. Let the color be the flame, and the whole horizon be the plate. Nothing to hold. Nothing to light. Just the original flame, and you in front of it. The bell holds the time.
Sunset without objects. Arti with nothing but the actual sun: face west, hands together, and watch the original flame go down. Today's word.
Your line: the original flame. Today, wherever you are at sunset, stop for one minute and face it. No objects needed. Day one hundred and twenty-three.

howItsDone: Many Hindus honor the sun directly, pouring water toward it at dawn or bowing to it at the twilight junctions; when no shrine is available, some simply face the rising or setting sun with folded hands.

what a scholar hears: Rig Veda 1.1 opens with praise of Agni as the priest of sacrifice; the Gayatri (RV 3.62.10) is addressed to Savitr, the solar deity; the sun is often called pratyaksha devata, the directly visible deity.

notes: Rig Veda 1.1 and the Gayatri are paraphrased, not quoted (Griffith 1896 is public domain but not on the validator's list).
'The god you can actually see' renders pratyaksha devata; confirm the phrase is commonly used of Surya.
The idea that the arti lamp is a 'stand-in' for the sun is an interpretive teaching, not a scriptural claim; confirm the framing is acceptable.
Safety line: never stare directly at the sun.
